problem: Choose one of four HackUMass XIV ideas (FocusPage, Crosscheck, Receipts, LectureLens) and note potential fixes for each; pivots/merges allowed.

agents.name: Agent A
agents.framing: Makes the strongest honest case for FocusPage (CVI picture books)

agents.name: Agent B
agents.framing: Makes the strongest honest case for Crosscheck (medication label verification)

agents.name: Agent C
agents.framing: Makes the strongest honest case for Receipts (transcript checker)

agents.name: Agent D
agents.framing: Makes the strongest honest case for LectureLens (course-aware captions)

agents.name: Agent F
agents.framing: Adversarial: failure modes, competitor overlap, ethics, demo risks

entries.response:
POSITION: Build FocusPage, the only idea whose output (a busy picture-book page visibly simplified for one specific child) demos in five seconds, runs on off-the-shelf parts, and can be evaluated with free synthetic ground truth.

WHY THIS IDEA WINS:
1. **Demo legibility.** A cluttered page becomes one red object on black, then flips to another child's profile instantly. Crosscheck's payoff is a spoken sentence, hard to show a room. LectureLens needs live audio in a loud hall where ASR gains look small. Receipts is a table diff, the demo judges have seen from Slate/EdVisorly.
2. **Thin competition.** Quick search found only manual or fixed-content tools: APH CVI Complexity Sequences (ten fixed image sets), Paths to Literacy CVI Book Builder (templates), Little Bear Sees (how-to guides), Vision Nanny. I found no tool that auto-adapts real books. Receipts faces EdVisorly/Parchment (100+ schools, 50k-transcript scale); Crosscheck faces Be My AI/Seeing AI (unverified); LectureLens faces custom-vocabulary ASR APIs.
3. **Most buildable.** Every stage is an API or library call: Gemini names the object, rembg/U2-Net (or hosted SAM 2) cuts it out, Pillow handles recolor, fade and outline. Cached cutouts make child/level switches instant, so the demo can't lag. Receipts needs two portals plus a rules engine; Crosscheck needs three witnesses plus a labeled benchmark; LectureLens needs streaming ASR.
4. **Free evaluation labels.** ARIA objects pasted on clutter give known masks (IoU, recognition retention); StoryWeaver is CC-BY. Crosscheck needs 40-60 hand-labeled photos; LectureLens needs 15 minutes of hand-corrected audio.
5. **Track fit and story.** Best Accessibility is the core target for a real population (2025 study: fatigue in over 90% of children with CVI, linked to clutter). Gemini is central, MongoDB holds profiles and cutouts, Vultr hosts it, and UI/UX is plausible.

WEAKNESSES I ADMIT:
- No CVI child tested, and clutter is only a proxy (the 2025 study found clutter metrics matched human ratings but did not predict fatigue). Expect a sharp judge to push here.
- Segmentation fails on multi-object pages, text-in-art, and thin or transparent objects, all common in picture books.
- The self-check is partly circular if Gemini both names and verifies, and an "unverified" flag on a good page looks bad live.
- Niche audience: the first 20 seconds must teach CVI.
- One unverified lead (a Google engineer's CVI literacy app) could undercut novelty; check it first.
- Copyright of adapted commercial books is unaddressed.

FIXES:
- Use a different model family as the verifier, and have it choose among distractors rather than free-name.
- Claim two measurable things only: object retention (IoU and recognition on ARIA) and monotonic clutter reduction. State plainly it is not a clinical outcome.
- Pre-adapt five StoryWeaver books for reliability, but keep a live path for a judge's pick.
- Open the pitch by showing a hand-cut, hand-recolored book next to the output.
- Email one TVI (Perkins, Anchor Center) before Saturday and quote them. This answers the disability-dongle critique that also hurts Crosscheck.
- Merge option: borrow Crosscheck's "show your uncertainty" idea so flagged pages become a feature, not a gap.

36H SCOPE:
- Demo-critical: StoryWeaver/PDF page ingest, Gemini subject naming, cutout with cache, levels L1-L4, two profiles, fullscreen viewer with teacher approve, verified badge, one rejected-page example, ARIA IoU results slide.
- Timeboxed: clutter metric (edge density or proto-object count, not full feature congestion).
- Cuttable: phone photo input, print export, accounts/login, batch-UI polish, SAVOIAS correlation, MongoDB beyond basic profile storage.
- Split: segmentation and levels pipeline; viewer and profile UI; eval and verifier; pitch, TVI outreach and data prep.

Sources: pathstoliteracy.org/resources/cvi-book-builder, aph.org/blog/create-custom-lessons-with-the-cvi-complexity-sequences-app, littlebearsees.org/2016/09/10/reducing-visual-complexity-books

POSITION: Build Crosscheck, because it is the only idea whose core claim ("an AI reader that says when it might be wrong") can be proven live, on a judge's own object, with a number attached, in a domain where a wrong answer is dangerous.

WHY THIS IDEA WINS:
1. The stakes are the clearest of the four. A misread "10 mg" vs "40 mg" is a safety event, so judges grasp it in one sentence. FocusPage is touching but its success metric (a proxy for clutter) is admittedly unvalidated with CVI children. LectureLens fixes an annoyance, and the gain on clean audio may be small. Receipts is a business pitch where judges ask "doesn't Slate or EdVisorly do this?" Crosscheck's claim is a measured silent-error count.
2. It has the strongest live-demo interaction. A judge picks a real bottle and the phone speaks the result. Then glare makes a single model say "40 mg" confidently while Crosscheck says "readers disagree on strength." Receipts is mostly a table and red cells. LectureLens is two caption panes, and the judge is a spectator. FocusPage is good, but its verification step is invisible.
3. It covers the most prize tracks with a real fit, not a stretch: Accessibility, MedTech (only Crosscheck truly qualifies), Most Impactful AI, Most Secure (in-memory only, visible in the network tab), UI/UX (VoiceOver-first), plus Claude and Gemini sponsors. The two-model design uses both sponsors for a reason, not as decoration.
4. Scope is the most controllable. There is no auth, no database, no two-sided portal, and no rules engine. The ensemble is three API calls plus about 150 lines of deterministic reconciliation. Receipts has two portals and a rules engine. LectureLens needs streaming ASR plus a correction pass.
5. Its evidence is deterministic and rerunnable: `make eval` on a held-out set shows counts, not vibes.

WEAKNESSES I ADMIT:
- Correlated errors. Claude and Gemini may misread the same glared label the same way. If so, the ensemble catches little and the pitch deflates.
- No blind user consulted. This is the "disability dongle" critique, and a judge may raise it.
- Novelty is unverified. My quick search found no evidence that Be My AI or Seeing AI report per-field confidence or cross-check models, but it also found no documentation either way. Treat "none do this" as unconfirmed, not as a fact. Do not say it on stage without checking their release notes.
- openFDA only confirms a strength exists for a drug. It cannot prove the label is read correctly. Docs show `active_ingredients` with strength strings like "500 mg/1", but I verified that only via third-party pages, not the official field reference.
- A 40-60 photo benchmark is small. Rates will have wide error bars, and "silent errors caught" may be a handful of cases.
- Safety framing. If it ever says "confirmed," someone may over-trust it.

FIXES:
- Counter correlation honestly. Make the thesis "disagreement is a signal, agreement is not proof." Report the agreed-but-wrong cases in the eval as a limitation. Add the OCR witness, since it fails differently from LLMs. Include degraded inputs deliberately, and show the correlated failures rather than hide them.
- Soften the wording. Say "readers agree" instead of "verified," and always end with "confirm with your pharmacist."
- Get one blind or low-vision tester. Contact UMass Disability Services or a local blind-services group Friday, or at minimum cite AFB and WebAIM and test the whole flow with VoiceOver on a team iPhone. Pre-register this as a limitation if no one is reachable.
- Check Be My AI and Seeing AI release notes in the first hour, and reword the pitch to "we measure and flag disagreement" if either has added a similar feature.
- Report counts with the denominator, for example "caught 9 of 11 silent errors; 2 false alarms in 40," and avoid percentages.
- Use fake-name printed labels and the team's own OTC bottles only, and say so.

36H SCOPE:
Demo-critical:
- Mobile web page with a camera or upload input and an aria-live results region.
- Claude and Gemini vision calls returning the same JSON schema.
- Deterministic reconciler (normalize units, compare fields, agree/disagree).
- Spoken uncertainty sentence.
- 40-60 photo benchmark with a CSV, a held-out split labeled Saturday afternoon, and `make eval`.
- A "single model vs Crosscheck" side-by-side on a glared bottle.
Cuttable, in order:
- Re-take guidance (glare/tilt).
- openFDA check.
- OCR witness. Cut this last of the three, since it counters the correlation risk.
- Eval dashboard UI (keep the CLI output).
Never cut: two-model reconciliation, spoken uncertainty, eval numbers, and the VoiceOver walkthrough.

POSITION: Build Receipts, but pitch it as a "show your work" transcript-to-GPA tool for one underserved wedge (international or non-standard transcripts), not as "the first to cross-check self-report."

WHY THIS IDEA WINS:
1. **The demo is the strongest and the most universal.** Any judge understands the red flag in five seconds: "Student said A in AP Chem, transcript says B+." FocusPage needs the judge to understand CVI phases. LectureLens needs a spoken mini-lecture and ears tuned to term errors. Crosscheck needs a medication label and trust in a benchmark. Receipts needs no domain explanation.
2. **It has the safest 36h build path.** The core is OCR/LLM extraction into a table, a diff, and deterministic Python GPA math. There is no segmentation model, no streaming ASR, and no multi-model ensemble. The engineering feedback ("compute in code, flag anomalies") makes it more robust than the other three, which depend on model quality that cannot be tuned on a deadline. A degraded demo still looks fine, because a messy table remains a table.
3. **Real pain and paying buyers.** Schools pay vendors today. FocusPage and LectureLens target budget-starved accessibility buyers. Receipts is a product people already buy. That helps with the Practicality criterion and gives a credible answer to "who uses this Monday?"
4. **Broad prize coverage.** It fits Most Impactful AI, Most Secure (in-memory processing, fake data only, audit log), Best UI/UX (the diff view), Gemini, MongoDB (the rules and audit log), and Best Overall. Crosscheck and FocusPage are more accessibility-concentrated, and they compete with each other for that same track.
5. **Auditable by design.** "Every number has a receipt" (click a GPA to see the source rows and rule) is a strong trust story and a good UI. It is also the right answer to the "AI shouldn't do the math" critique.

WEAKNESSES I ADMIT:
- **My own search undercut our key claim.** EdVisorly's EddyVerify markets automated comparison of self-reported data against the official transcript, course by course, with humans reviewing only flagged mismatches. That is almost exactly our headline differentiator. "First to cross-check" is false and a judge could find it in one search. (Vendor marketing only. I found no independent accuracy data.) STARS EasyImport is confirmed as AI import for the student's self-report, in beta, with no checking step.
- Innovation is the weakest of the four. This is a crowded, solved-ish category.
- Scope creep risk: two portals, a rules engine, AI classification, and a diff.
- Slow university sales, FERPA, and the question of who pays on the student side.
- Extraction accuracy on real, messy transcripts is untested. We can only use fake ones.

FIXES:
- **Drop "first." Lead with transparency and a wedge.** The pitch: "Incumbents give you a number. Receipts gives you a number you can audit, and it handles the transcripts they struggle with." Pick one wedge: international or non-standard transcripts (different grade scales, credit systems, course names), or small schools without Slate-scale budgets. Then demo a transcript on a non-US scale.
- **Collapse to one screen.** One app with a "student" and "school" tab, not two portals. A shared extraction pipeline feeds both.
- **Make the AI classification the hero.** The admissions feedback calls it the hard, valuable part. Show a course-name classifier with confidence and a checkbox for override. Rules live as one JSON preset.
- **Measure it.** Build a 15 to 20 fake-transcript benchmark with known ground truth (varied layouts, scanned or rotated). Report field accuracy and anomaly-detection rate. This answers "doesn't EdVisorly do this?" with numbers instead of claims, and it matches the evaluation rigor of Crosscheck.
- Add an override audit log (cheap, high value to admissions staff).

36H SCOPE:
- **Demo-critical:** (1) upload a fake transcript, then extract into an editable table; (2) student self-report vs official diff, mismatches in red; (3) one JSON preset with grade conversion and "Calculate GPA" in Python, with a click-to-trace receipt for each number; (4) AI course classification with override checkboxes; (5) a small accuracy benchmark slide.
- **Cuttable:** the second preset, the anomaly flags beyond one or two (credit outlier, printed GPA mismatch), sorting, and the audit log (cut last, since it is cheap). Also cut any real auth, multi-tenant setup, and Slate-style integrations.
- **Never cut:** deterministic math, the red diff, the receipt trace, and one honest accuracy number.

POSITION: Build LectureLens, because its core claim (course-aware captions beat stock captions on course terms) can be proven live, on a fresh clip, with a number, using one cheap API call, so it carries the least build risk of the four.

WHY THIS IDEA WINS:
1. Lowest technical risk, knowable by hour 2. Deepgram (Nova-3/Flux `keyterm`, up to ~100 terms) and AssemblyAI (streaming `keyterms_prompt`, ~100 terms) document keyword boosting, so the biased-ASR core is one parameter on a hosted API. FocusPage chains segmentation, two vision models, a clutter metric and profiles. Receipts needs two portals plus a rules engine. Crosscheck needs a labeled photo benchmark plus three-witness reconciliation.
2. The demo is self-evident. Two panes, same audio: stock says "Dyke's trah" and "heap a fly"; ours says "Dijkstra" and "heapify". A judge can say a term and watch. Receipts' payoff is a table diff judges have seen; FocusPage's payoff (a child with CVI recognizing the object) cannot be shown in the room.
3. Falsifiable measured claim: term error rate across baseline, glossary prompt, and prompt plus correction, including false corrections introduced, rerun on a clip recorded at the table.
4. Real users and a legal tailwind: Deaf and hard-of-hearing students, and the ADA Title II web accessibility rule for large public universities. Real UMass CICS syllabi also target Best UMass Hack.
5. Honest differentiation: boosting itself is a commodity vendor feature. My search found Otter has a manual custom vocabulary (2019 launch, paid tiers) and Panopto has a site-level admin dictionary (Aalto emails words to be added). I found no evidence either builds a vocabulary automatically from a student's own syllabus or slides. That gap (automatic, per-course, student-controlled) is the claim.

WEAKNESSES I ADMIT:
- Thin moat: a vendor could add "upload your syllabus" in a sprint.
- Gain on clean speech may be small; modern ASR handles "heap" and "stack". The lift is in rare terms, names, accents.
- The benchmark (15 min hand-corrected) is hours of labor, and a teammate-recorded set invites overfitting doubts.
- No Deaf user input, so the disability-dongle critique applies; a few points of term accuracy is incremental.
- A correction pass adds latency, and caption lag is a top Deaf-user complaint.
- Visually the least flashy: text on a screen.

FIXES:
- Pitch it as a course-aware layer on any ASR, not a new ASR. Say upfront that boosting is a vendor feature; our contribution is auto-extraction, measurement, and flagging uncertainty.
- Build an adversarial benchmark: dense rare terms (Dijkstra, heapify, amortized, Kruskal), two fast or non-native speakers, some noise. Report TER and false corrections. A null result on clean audio is fine if stated.
- Constrain the correction pass to substitutions near glossary terms (edit or phonetic distance), each with a confidence score, instead of free LLM rewriting.
- Show low-confidence fixes with a dotted underline. This borrows Crosscheck's "say when unsure" strength.
- Contact UMass Disability Services or one Deaf/HoH student by Saturday morning and quote them on the slide.
- Merge option: LectureLens plus Crosscheck's uncertainty framing, as one "AI that shows its uncertainty to accessibility users" story.

36H SCOPE:
Demo-critical: (1) syllabus/slide PDF to editable glossary; (2) streaming ASR with keyterm boost beside a stock pane on the same audio; (3) benchmark script for WER and TER across three setups, plus a results slide; (4) clean two-pane UI with highlighted corrected terms.
Nice to have: constrained correction with confidence flags; preloaded CICS syllabus.
Cuttable: tap-for-definition, true streaming (3-second chunks are fine), speaker labels, accounts, mobile.

Sources: developers.deepgram.com/docs/keyterm; assemblyai.com/blog/streaming-keyterms-prompting; nojitter.com/ai-speech-technologies/otterai-adds-custom-vocabulary; blogs.aalto.fi/opit/?p=1553

SCORECARD (1-10; total is the sum of all five columns, max 50)

| Idea | Innovation | Functionality | Practicality | Presentation | Demo memorability | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A: FocusPage | 8 | 7 | 7 | 8 | 9 | 39 |
| B: Crosscheck | 6 | 8 | 7 | 8 | 8 | 37 |
| C: Receipts | 4 | 6 | 7 | 6 | 6 | 29 |
| D: LectureLens | 5 | 7 | 6 | 7 | 6 | 31 |

Notes behind the numbers: FocusPage is the only one where a judge says "I haven't seen that." The cutout cache with a per-child dial is a real system, not a prompt. Crosscheck has the cleanest measured claim ("N silent errors, X caught"), but multi-model agreement is a known pattern. Receipts is the weakest on Innovation because EdVisorly and Parchment already exist, and its scope is the largest. LectureLens's gain on clean audio may be small, and a live ASR demo in a loud hall is fragile.

CREDIBLE PRIZES (can win, not merely enter)
- FocusPage: Best Accessibility (strong contender), Best UI/UX, Gemini sponsor. Most Impactful AI is plausible. MongoDB is a stretch (profile storage only). Best Overall is a long shot unless the demo lands perfectly.
- Crosscheck: Best Accessibility, MedTech, Most Impactful AI, and the Claude and Gemini sponsor prizes (it uses both). Best Overall is plausible. Most Secure is weak: "we don't store anything" is a claim, not a security design.
- Receipts: Gemini sponsor and maybe MongoDB. Most Impactful AI and Most Secure are not credible. It would enter many categories and win none.
- LectureLens: Best Accessibility, Best Software Hack, and Best UMass Hack (only with real CICS syllabi). Most Impactful AI is possible if the numbers are dramatic.

TOP FIX PER IDEA
- FocusPage: Get one real TVI or CVI professional (Perkins, Anchor Center, a UMass special-ed contact) to look at about 5 adapted pages and give one sentence of feedback. Put it on the slide. "No CVI children tested" is survivable, but "no practitioner has seen this" is not. Also cut scope to L1-L3 if the L4 outline is eating time.
- Crosscheck: Lock the headline metric before building the UI: "of N confident-but-wrong reads by the single model, the ensemble flagged X, with Y false alarms." Spend one hour with a VoiceOver user. That answers both the correlated-error and "disability dongle" critiques.
- Receipts: Cut it to the single moment that wins: the self-report vs. transcript diff with a GPA that shows its work. Drop the student portal and the rules engine. Add a wedge, such as international transcripts, so "doesn't Slate do this?" has an answer.
- LectureLens: Use hard audio (accented speakers, a noisy room, dense vocabulary) so the baseline visibly fails. Report term error rate, including false corrections. A visibly broken baseline is the whole demo.

CURRENT PICK
FocusPage, narrowly over Crosscheck. At a table, I remember the judge picking a book, watching it adapt live, seeing a "verified: still recognized as dog" badge, and then seeing a page get rejected. That is a visual, interactive demo with a self-checking mechanism, and the CVI niche is specific enough to feel real instead of generic "AI for accessibility." The cached cutout and the complexity dial are real engineering beyond an API call, which answers the "AI wrapper" objection. Its weakness is the lack of validation: the clutter metric is only a proxy, and no children were tested. It is also the heaviest build (Gemini, segmentation, a second vision model, a clutter metric, an evaluation), so the scope risk is real. Crosscheck is the safer 36-hour build with the tighter metric, and it loses mainly on Innovation and on live-photo fragility. Receipts and LectureLens trail clearly. Merge note: both A and B rely on "a second model checks the first," so that idea can be a shared thread in the pitch.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND
If FocusPage segmentation and recognition retention fail on the 200-object ARIA test by Saturday midday, or no practitioner will give feedback, I would switch to Crosscheck.

**FATAL-IF-UNFIXED**

- **FocusPage:** The self-check is circular. A vision model confirming "still a dog" tells you nothing about whether a child with CVI can process the page, and the write-up admits no CVI child was tested. Judges and TVIs will read "verified" as a clinical claim. Fix: rename the badge "object still recognizable (machine check)" and never say "safe" or "CVI-approved". Get one TVI, or the Perkins or CVI Book Nook community, to react to the output before Sunday. Keep the 2-minute demo on the cached-cutout speed and the L1-L4 dial, and drop the live photo-of-a-page path unless it is rock solid.
- **Crosscheck:** Correlated errors plus a medication-harm framing. If Claude and Gemini both misread the same glared label, the screen says "two readers agree" and the user takes the wrong dose. "Confirmed" is the most dangerous word in the app. Fix: never output "confirmed" or "safe". Say "readers agree; verify with your pharmacist." Report the silent-error rate that survives the ensemble, including cases where all witnesses agreed and were wrong, and put that number on a slide. Add one hard rule: if the OCR witness lacks the strength string, the app never says "agree." Talk to at least one blind user or an org rep before Saturday.
- **Receipts:** Its central claim is false. EdVisorly's EddyVerify (their own pages) already compares self-reported application data against official transcripts course by course and flags discrepancies, and EddyAI recalculates GPAs using institution rules. "First to cross-check" will get you caught on the first judge question. Fix: drop "first." Wedge on something they don't do, such as international or non-standard transcripts, or a per-number "receipt" UI that links each figure to a pixel region of the source document. Scope is also fatal: two portals plus a rules engine plus a diff is too much for 36 hours. Cut it to one flow: upload, extract, diff, show your work.
- **LectureLens:** The gain may be small, and the vendors already do this. Otter has had Custom Vocabulary since 2019, Verbit offers custom dictionaries and a live product, Panopto has custom dictionaries, and cloud ASR has phrase hints. Your novelty is auto-building the glossary from a syllabus plus the term-error benchmark. On clean CS speech modern ASR may already get these terms mostly right, so the demo could show no visible difference. Fix: run the baseline on your actual speakers and clips by Friday night. If the gap is under about 10 points of term error rate, pivot to messy audio (accents, mic distance), or merge into a different idea.

**OTHER RISKS**

FocusPage
- Segmentation fails on stylized illustrations (overlapping characters, text in the art). The demo only works on books you pre-tested. Know which books those are.
- The "clutter decreases monotonically" claim is trivially satisfiable and can be gamed. Clutter metrics didn't predict fatigue (their own cited study).
- Disability-dongle risk is moderate: the tool is for teachers, and nobody who has CVI has seen it.

Crosscheck
- Wifi risk: two cloud models plus openFDA means three network dependencies live. One 10-second latency spike or rate limit kills a 60-second demo. Prepare cached fallbacks and a video.
- Using real pill bottles and an unsupervised health claim: the demo must say it's a prototype and not medical advice.
- A benchmark of 40-60 photos, mostly team-made mock labels, is too small to support accuracy claims. Report raw counts with no percentages.

Receipts
- Real transcripts are FERPA-sensitive, so you are limited to fake ones. Extraction accuracy on fake transcripts proves little, and judges know it.
- Moat claim (configurable rules) is exactly what EdVisorly sells with 100+ schools.
- The unanswered "who pays for the student side?" question was raised in the prior feedback.

LectureLens
- Streaming ASR plus a correction pass is a latency trap. Caption lag is the problem you cite, and a correction pass adds lag.
- An LLM correction pass can hallucinate "fixes" that put wrong words in a deaf student's captions. The false-correction count must be reported.
- No Deaf or HoH student was consulted. The write-up is built on citations, not users.

**CLAIMS THAT NEED VERIFYING**
- Receipts: "first to cross-check self-report vs transcript" is contradicted by EddyVerify. Also "99% accuracy" and "95%+ at UT Austin" are vendor claims.
- Crosscheck: "none report confidence or cross-check models" is still unverified. My search found no Be My AI or Seeing AI confidence feature, but that is absence of evidence, not proof. Check the app release notes directly.
- LectureLens: "student-controlled glossary" as differentiator. Otter's custom vocabulary is per-account, so students can already add terms. Only the auto-build from a syllabus is plausibly new.
- FocusPage: no AI CVI-simplification tool turned up in my search (the only AI mention was a forward-looking one), which supports novelty. But CVI Book Nook and Little Bear Sees already supply pre-adapted material. Also verify the "leading cause" and "90% fatigue" figures against the cited papers.
- Crosscheck: the WebAIM mobile and iOS percentages need a source check. Also the openFDA endpoints "still to be checked."

**LEAST-RISKY IDEA:** FocusPage. Competitors are manual, with no AI incumbent found. Failures are graceful (a bad cutout is visible and the teacher approves each page). It has no safety-critical output, and caching makes the demo fast and resistant to latency. The main risk is overclaiming "verified."

**MOST-RISKY IDEA:** Receipts. It has the most scope, the false "first" claim, strong incumbents that hold the exact feature, a slow-sales market, and fake data that makes accuracy claims weak. Crosscheck is a close second on harm potential, but its risk is manageable through wording and framing. Receipts' risk is structural.

AGREEMENTS:
- Critic (F), strongest counterargument: the self-check is circular and "verified" reads as a clinical claim. A vision model saying "still a dog" says nothing about whether a child with CVI can process the page. Conceded in full. The badge becomes "object still recognizable (machine check)". We never write "safe" or "CVI-approved". The verifier is a different model family and picks from distractors instead of free-naming. Calling it "verified" was my overreach.
- Judge (E): FocusPage is the heaviest build (Gemini, segmentation, verifier, clutter metric, eval), and my "most buildable" claim was too strong. Crosscheck is the safer 36h build. Pipeline stages are API calls, but integration and segmentation failure on stylized art are real risks.
- Crosscheck advocate (B): the verification step is invisible on screen. True, and I will make it visible (see proposal).
- LectureLens advocate (D): a child's recognition can't be shown in the room. True. We show retention and clutter numbers instead, and say plainly that this is not a clinical outcome.
- Receipts advocate (C) and Critic (F): Receipts' "first" claim is dead. Receipts should drop out unless it takes the international-transcript wedge.
- Crosscheck's "correlated errors plus medication harm" risk is structural, and I accept the Critic's ranking of risk. The Critic's own conclusion (FocusPage is least risky, no safety-critical output) cuts in our favor.
- E's mind-changer is fair: if ARIA segmentation or retention fails by Saturday midday, we switch to Crosscheck.

DISAGREEMENTS:
- F's claim that "clutter decreases monotonically" is trivially satisfiable. Partly agree, so I demote it. The headline claim is object retention on 200 ARIA objects pasted on clutter (IoU plus recognition), where ground truth is free. Clutter reduction is a sanity check only.
- B says Crosscheck's demo is stronger because the judge picks a bottle. Wifi risk and glare variance make a live photo fragile, a point F made against Crosscheck. FocusPage's cached cutouts make the judge-picks-a-book demo latency-proof. A wrong answer in a med-label demo is also a safety story, while a bad cutout is merely visible and teacher-rejectable.
- D and B call FocusPage's payoff invisible. It is the most visible of the four. A busy page collapses to one red object on black, then flips to another child's profile. That demos in 5 seconds, with no explanation of CVI phases beyond one slide.

REFINED PROPOSAL:
Scope down to demo-critical and make uncertainty visible, the best merge from the debate.
- Core: StoryWeaver/PDF ingest, Gemini subject naming, cached cutout, levels L1-L3 (L4 only if time), two child profiles, fullscreen viewer with teacher approve.
- Borrowed from Crosscheck: the "machine check" shows a confidence state per page (recognizable / uncertain / multi-object, teacher review). A flagged page becomes a feature, not a gap. Multi-object and text-in-art pages are flagged, not forced.
- Evidence slide: ARIA retention counts with denominators (for example "recognized on 171 of 200"), one rejected example, and an honest-limits box.
- Pitch opens with a hand-cut, hand-recolored book beside the output.
- Pre-adapt 5 tested books. Keep the live path for a judge's pick, but only on books from a pre-tested list.
- Cut: phone photo, print, login, SAVOIAS, MongoDB beyond profiles.

FIXES UPDATE:

FINAL PIPELINE:
1. Ingest: PyMuPDF renders each page to PNG. StoryWeaver pages are images already.
2. One Gemini call (Flash, JSON schema) returns: main_subject name, a bounding box (Gemini's native 0-1000 box output), list_of_other_objects, and flags multi_object and text_in_art. This is the name-to-mask link. The name and box come from the same call.
3. Cutout: SAM 2 prompted with that box (hosted via Replicate, or vit_b on Vultr). Budget 3 hours. Fallback if SAM slips: crop to the Gemini box, then run rembg (isnet-anime) inside the crop. The box forces the right object.
4. Render: L1 is a luminance-preserving tint (shading and internal edges kept) of the child's hue on black. It is not a flat fill. L2 is real colors on plain. L3 is faded scene plus vivid object. Cached cutouts make switching instant.

Checks that catch real failures:
- C1 mask-box sanity: IoU(mask bbox, Gemini box) at least 0.6. This catches the wrong object.
- C2 geometric sanity: mask area 3-70% of the page, one component holding at least 90% of the area, and the mask not touching 3 or more page edges. This catches background leak and fragments.
- C3 cross-family verifier (Claude, since Claude is a possible sponsor): it sees only the L1 render. The choices are the target plus the page's other objects from step 2 (not random words). If the cut grabbed the tree instead of the dog, it picks "tree" and fails.
- C4 L1 recognizability: if the verifier recognizes L2 but not L1, that page auto-falls back to L2 and says so on screen.
- Any failure, or a multi_object or text_in_art flag, shows a "teacher review" card. This is the visible-uncertainty feature.

Evidence: teammates hand-box 20 real StoryWeaver pages (about 40 minutes). Report the Gemini-vs-hand box IoU and counts of accepted / flagged / failed (for example "14 / 4 / 2 of 20"). Headline claim: "recognizable by machine check on X of 20". It is not a clinical claim.
